About MRDS

About Mercy Rural Development Society

Mercy Rural Development Society (MRDS) is a registered society working towards rural community development and empowerment.

Our approach centres on strengthening communities, encouraging collective participation and supporting pathways towards sustainable and self-reliant livelihoods.

  • Community Participation
  • Women’s Empowerment
  • Collective Action
  • Sustainable Development
  • Rural Livelihoods
  • Inclusive Growth
Learn More About MRDS
Areas of Development

Our Work

Building stronger rural communities through participation, collective action and sustainable development.

Rural Community Development

Supporting community-led development and strengthening rural participation.

Women’s Empowerment

Encouraging women’s participation, collective action and opportunities for greater self-reliance.

Self-Help Groups

Supporting community groups and collective structures that help strengthen local participation and livelihoods.

Sustainable Livelihoods

Promoting pathways that can help rural communities build more sustainable economic opportunities.

Community Capacity Building

Strengthening knowledge, participation and collective decision-making within communities.

Social Development

Working towards inclusive and sustainable development at the grassroots level.

Why Community Partnership Matters

What guides our approach

Five commitments that shape how MRDS works alongside rural communities.

Grassroots Approach

Development begins by understanding communities and their needs.

Community Participation

Encouraging people to actively participate in their own development.

Collective Strength

Supporting community groups and collective action.

Sustainable Focus

Prioritising long-term empowerment rather than short-term assistance.

Local Engagement

Maintaining a strong connection with rural communities.

Impact Begins With People

Every group formed represents people choosing to work together for a stronger, more self-reliant community.

Across the communities MRDS works with, 130 groups have been formed, of which 94 remain active today — bringing together 1,658 active members.

These figures reflect the organisation’s established network of community groups, built through sustained engagement and collective participation at the grassroots level.

These numbers represent MRDS’s community-group network, not a total beneficiary count.
